intro: Grieg’s Wedding Day at Troldhaugen, Op. 65 No. 6, opens with a march, and its middle section is a quiet duet. Harald Vetter plays the piece, which ends on a single blunt chord.

sections.label: A · March in D major
sections.mNote: Low octaves, short detached chords and a quick triplet figure.

sections.label: B · March theme in full chords
sections.mNote: The tune returns in octaves and full chords.

sections.label: C · Duet in G major
sections.mNote: The melody passes between the pianist’s hands.

sections.label: D · Opening march, D major, Tempo I
sections.mNote: The opening march returns at Tempo I.

sections.label: E · Triplets at ppp, final fff chord
sections.mNote: The piano drops to ppp, then plays a final fff chord.

cues.title: Opening march
cues.text: Grieg marked the piece Tempo di Marcia un poco vivace. The left hand plays a low D beneath short chords, and a quick triplet leads into the melody.
cues.evidence: Grieg, Op. 65 No. 6, bars 1–10, Louis Oesterle edition, typeset by David Whipple for Mutopia: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/GriegE/O65/troldhaugen/troldhaugen-a4.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Silver wedding at Troldhaugen
cues.text: At Grieg’s silver wedding anniversary, more guests came to Troldhaugen than he and Nina had invited. He wrote this piece in the summer of 1896. Its first title was “The well-wishers are coming”.
cues.evidence: Ernst-Günter Heinemann and Einar Steen-Nøkleberg, preface to Henle HN 1291 (2016), pp. III–IV: silver wedding, unexpected guests, composition in summer 1896 and autograph title “Die Gratulanten kommen”, translated here. https://www.henle.de/media/cb/cd/75/1697725893/1291-1697725893-sync.pdf

cues.title: Middle section in G major
cues.text: The march gives way to G major in 2/4, marked Poco tranquillo. A cantando melody passes between the pianist’s hands over soft chords. The busy bass of the opening stops.
cues.evidence: Oesterle edition, bars 57–106: G major, 2/4, Poco tranquillo and cantando melody.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter from Hinrichsen, 1904
cues.text: On 21 December 1904 the publisher Henri Hinrichsen wrote to Grieg that Wedding Day and the earlier Lyric Pieces were still much played and sold “like hotcakes”.
cues.evidence: Hinrichsen to Grieg, 21 December 1904, quoted in the Henle HN 1291 preface, p. III, from Benestad and Brock, Edvard Grieg: Briefwechsel mit dem Musikverlag C. F. Peters 1863–1907 (1997), p. 550. “Wie warme Semmeln” is translated here as “like hotcakes”. https://www.henle.de/media/cb/cd/75/1697725893/1291-1697725893-sync.pdf

cues.title: Return of the opening march
cues.text: D major returns at bar 107 with Tempo I. The low octaves, clipped chords and triplet of the opening march are heard again in their original places, after the quiet duet.
cues.evidence: Oesterle edition, bar 107 onwards: return to D major, 4/4 and Tempo I, followed by the opening material.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda and final chord
cues.text: Triplets continue over low D octaves as the dynamic falls from p to pp and then ppp, with the soft pedal down. The piece ends on a single D major chord marked fff.
cues.evidence: Oesterle edition, bars 163 to the end: D pedal, triplets, unacorda, ppp and final fff chord with tre corde.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Son of a Bergen merchant; used Norwegian fiddle tunes, a troll king and a wedding party in concert-hall music.
facts: Conductor in Christiania, 1866–74 · Harmonien, Bergen, 1880–82 · a state composer’s stipend from 1874
Rikard Nordraak 1864–65 · Piano Concerto 1869 · Peer Gynt 1876 · Troldhaugen 1885
Ten books of Lyric Pieces, about 170 songs, a piano concerto, stage music, a string quartet and five sonatas

quote.text: The most important thing is truth, the truth of feeling.
quote.source: Grieg to Julius Röntgen, May 1904, quoted in Finn Benestad, Norsk biografisk leksikon

composer.background:
Edvard Grieg was born on 15 June 1843 in the family house at Strandgaten 152, above Bergen’s harbour. His father, Alexander, was a merchant and the British vice-consul; his mother, Gesine, who had studied singing, piano and theory in Hamburg, taught him the piano from the age of six. He hated scales. In his essay Min første Succes he recalled the day at five when he stretched up to the keyboard and found a third, a triad, a four-note chord and at last, with both hands, the five notes of a ninth. “That was a success!” he wrote. “Nothing since has been able to intoxicate me like this.”

In the summer of 1858 the violinist Ole Bull called without warning at the Griegs’ summer house at Landås. Edvard was made to play. Bull grew serious, talked quietly with the parents, then shook the boy in his own way and said: “You are going to Leipzig to become an artist!” On 6 October Grieg entered the Conservatory. He later called it “that damned Leipzig conservatory”, but he went free to the Gewandhaus rehearsals, saw Tannhäuser fourteen times, and heard Clara Schumann play her husband’s concerto. In the spring of 1860 tuberculosis ruined one of his lungs. That autumn, against the doctor’s advice, he went back.
